why: Pain can affect thoughts, emotions, and actions—and those responses can affect participation and distress. CBT skills help you notice that cycle and choose a more useful response.

slides.title: Pain Is Real
slides.content: Using a psychological skill does not mean pain is imaginary. Persistent symptoms affect the whole person, and whole-person care can include cognitive and behavioural tools.

slides.title: Notice the Cycle
slides.content: A symptom may trigger a thought, emotion, body response, and action. For example: pain, then fear, then bracing or avoidance, then less confidence.

slides.title: Check the Thought
slides.content: Ask whether the thought is a fact, a prediction, or one possible interpretation. Look for a response that is accurate without dismissing the difficulty.

slides.title: Choose a Useful Action
slides.content: A useful action might be adjusting the task, using a coping strategy, asking for support, or completing a manageable part of the activity.

slides.title: Try It Once
slides.content: Write one difficult thought from this week. Then write a more balanced statement and one action that supports your goals.
